<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust–Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Amit Sarker
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Moumita Choudhury
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Saaduddin Mahmud
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Shlomo Zilberstein
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>University of Massachusetts Amherst
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Email: </span><a href="mailto:"><span id="id1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">{asarker, amchoudhury, smahmud, shlomo}@umass.edu</span></a>
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly participate in negotiations on behalf of individuals and organizations, yet they remain vulnerable to manipulation, particularly in repeated multi-party interactions.
Classical multi-agent systems address this challenge through explicit trust and reputation models, whereas existing work on LLM negotiation largely treats trust as an emergent phenomenon.
We investigate whether LLM agents can form useful trust estimates from prior interactions and leverage them to improve future negotiation outcomes.
We introduce a repeated, multi-party, multi-issue negotiation framework in which recurring agents participate in a sequence of negotiation games while one participant covertly attempts to prevent agreement.
After each game, agents assess their counterparts and maintain pairwise trust estimates that carry over to subsequent negotiations.
We compare trust-aware and trust-agnostic agents and analyze how explicit trust influences negotiation outcomes.
Our results reveal a <em id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">trust–agreement gap</em>: trust-aware agents can identify the adversary within a few games, but accurate trust estimates do not consistently translate into better agreements.
Trust increases agreement rates by up to 23 percentage points, but only when agents are explicitly guided to use it in their decisions. Explicit trust can therefore improve repeated LLM negotiations, but its value depends critically on how trust is assessed and incorporated into agents’ reasoning.</p>
  
</div>

</span>

<div id="p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="p3.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Keywords</em> Multi-party negotiation, LLMs, Trust</p>
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Large language models (LLMs) have evolved beyond chatbots that generate isolated responses.
LLMs can interact with tools, combine reasoning with actions, and participate in complex multi-turn workflows.
Multi-agent LLM systems extend these capabilities by enabling agents to communicate and coordinate as part of a larger decision-making process <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>, <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>]</cite>.
As these systems mature, LLM agents will increasingly act on behalf of individuals and organizations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>, <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite>.
Emerging applications already employ LLMs in contract discussions and automated supplier negotiations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>]</cite>.
Negotiation is therefore becoming a core capability for LLM agents: tasks such as allocating resources, negotiating contracts, and approving projects require prolonged deliberation among parties with different objectives <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>.
To succeed in such settings, agents must remain robust when counterparts behave strategically or adversarially—for example, by using persuasion, concealing information, or attempting to manipulate the negotiation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>, <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We study this problem in multi-party scorable negotiation games <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite>, in which a group of organizations engages in repeated negotiations (Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust–Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>).
In each game, a company proposes a project and negotiates its terms with a funding ministry, local communities, and advocacy groups.
The parties deliberate over a set of issues, such as budget, location, and compensation, where each issue has several options, and a deal assigns one option to every issue.
Every party privately scores the options according to its own priorities and accepts only deals that meet its minimum threshold.
As the same parties meet again over new projects, each negotiation leaves behind evidence of who compromised, who obstructed, and who was reliable.
Now suppose one participant covertly benefits if no agreement is reached: it can reject reasonable deals, push proposals others will oppose, and disguise obstruction as principled bargaining.
A human negotiator in this situation would rely on trust built from past encounters to decide whose proposals to support and whose objections to discount.
The central question we investigate is whether LLM agents can form and leverage such trust.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2610.31971v1/teaser_figure_arxiv.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/233;" width="476" height="233" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span><span id="S1.F1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Repeated multi-party negotiation with explicit trust.</span>
Five parties negotiate a package over five issues with four options each; a deal needs four of the five votes.
Each party holds private (<span id="S1.F1.5" class="ltx_text" style="position:relative; bottom:-1.2pt;"><img src="2610.31971v1/Figures/lock_icon.png" id="S1.F1.g3" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:10/12;" width="10" height="12" alt="Refer to caption"></span>) scores, minimum threshold to accept (BATNA, <math id="S1.F1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math>), and a trust vector with one entry per counterpart.
One party covertly prefers no agreement.
After every game, each party updates trust with BRS, rubric-based, or free-form assessment, and the updated trust carries into the next game.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Prior work shows why this question matters.
LLM negotiators exhibit a limited range of strategies, accept unfavorable offers, and remain vulnerable to adversarial persuasion <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>, <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>, <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>]</cite>.
These weaknesses become even more pronounced in repeated multi-party interactions, where a single strategic or adversarial participant can influence otherwise cooperative agents, steer the final agreement, or form a coalition against another stakeholder <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>. Classical multi-agent systems address this challenge through explicit trust and reputation mechanisms, which estimate the reliability of counterparts from prior interactions and use these estimates to guide subsequent decisions under uncertainty <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>, <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite>.
However, existing work on LLM negotiation largely treats trust as an emergent phenomenon to be observed rather than as information that agents explicitly use when making decisions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite>.
Consequently, it remains unclear whether LLM agents can form useful trust estimates from prior negotiations and leverage them to improve future outcomes.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To investigate this question, we introduce <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">TASMAN</span> (<span id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">T</span>rust-<span id="S1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A</span>ugmented <span id="S1.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">S</span>trategic <span id="S1.p4.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">M</span>ulti-<span id="S1.p4.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A</span>gent <span id="S1.p4.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">N</span>egotiation), a <em id="S1.p4.1.8" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">repeated</em> negotiation setting in which trust formed in one game informs the next.
After each game, agents assess their counterparts with one of three methods: the beta reputation system (BRS) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite>, where the LLM reports feedback and a Bayesian rule computes trust; rubric-based trust, where the LLM scores each counterpart on five predefined behavioral metrics; or free-form judgment, where the LLM chooses its own criteria.
Agents carry these scores into the next game, with or without guidance on how to use them.
We address four research questions:</p>
<ul id="S1.p4.2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RQ1—Trust formation:</span> Can LLM agents form trust from negotiation history that distinguishes a covert adversary from cooperative counterparts, and how does this trust evolve over repeated negotiations?</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RQ2—Trust assessment:</span> Which assessment method produces more reliable trust: BRS adapted for LLMs, a predefined rubric, or the LLM’s own criteria?</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RQ3—Negotiation outcomes:</span> When does explicit trust improve negotiation outcomes, and how much of its value do agents leave unused (<em id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">trust–agreement gap</em>)?</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RQ4—Agent reasoning:</span> How does explicit trust change what agents reason about when they propose and vote?</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Our contributions are threefold.
First, we introduce <span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">TASMAN</span>, a repeated multi-party negotiation framework in which agents form trust that carries over between games and explicitly informs their decisions.
Second, we adapt the classical reputation model BRS to LLM agents.
Third, we define the <em id="S1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">trust–agreement gap</em>, which measures the agreement an agent loses by not using its trust as well as possible.
Our results show that trust-aware agents identify the adversary within a few games.
The best assessment method depends on the LLM, but BRS detects the adversary reliably in every condition.
Without guidance, however, this accurate trust does not significantly improve outcomes over trust-agnostic agents.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Automated negotiation in multi-agent systems.</span>  
Automated negotiation spans bargaining theory <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>, <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>; game-theoretic, heuristic, and argumentation-based agents <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>, <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>, <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>, <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>]</cite>; and, under incomplete information, opponent modeling, and learned bidding and acceptance policies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>, <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>, <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>, <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite>.
However, these systems represent offers as points in a predefined utility space, which do not capture the strategic behaviors that emerge in natural language.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Trust and reputation models.</span>  
Trust and reputation have been recognized as central to effective interaction in open multi-agent systems, where self-interested agents may defect or misrepresent their behavior <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>, <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>]</cite>.
Models such as FIRE and TRAVOS estimate counterpart reliability from previous interactions and use these estimates to guide partner selection and decisions under uncertainty <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>, <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>]</cite>.
For LLM agents, RepuNet maintains peer reputations in social dilemmas <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite>, and RHM adapts policies to opponent models in two-player repeated games <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite>.
We bring explicit trust to repeated multi-party negotiation, where prior work treats trust mainly as an emergent phenomenon <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LLM agents and negotiation.</span>  
Automated negotiation has progressed from neural dialogue systems that learn bargaining strategies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>, <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite> to human-level performance in Diplomacy by combining language models with strategic planning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>, <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite>.
LLM agents can generate offers, respond to other parties, and improve their strategies through self-play or feedback <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>.
However, evaluations identify limited strategic diversity, acceptance of dominated offers, and susceptibility to adversarial tactics <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>, <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>, <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>]</cite> and multi-agent studies report vulnerability to deception, manipulation, and coordination failures <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>, <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>, <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite>.
Closest to our work, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abdelnabi et al. [1]</a></cite> introduce multi-party negotiation games with cooperative, greedy and adversarial variants.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Problem Formulation</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We study repeated multi-party negotiation, in which the same group of LLM agents participates in a sequence of multi-issue negotiation games.
Our setting builds on the framework of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abdelnabi et al. [1]</a></cite>, with changes to the interaction protocol that allow trust formed in one game to carry over to subsequent negotiation decisions.
In their protocol, each negotiation is self-contained: a designated proposer starts the negotiation with its preferred deal, agents exchange support or counter-proposals for a fixed number of rounds, and the same proposer selects the final deal, which is then checked against each party’s private acceptance threshold.
In our setting, agents engage in a sequence of negotiation games, and every proposal is followed by a voting round.
The first proposal to receive the required number of votes becomes the agreement; if no proposal does, the game ends without a deal after a finite number of rounds.
An agreement is therefore determined directly by the votes cast for it, and the number of rounds needed to reach one is itself a measurable outcome.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Repeated Negotiation Game</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{N}=\{1,\ldots,n\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{N}=\{1,\ldots,n\}</annotation></semantics></math> be the set of parties.
The same parties participate in a sequence of negotiation episodes<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
              
              
              
            We use games and episodes interchangeably in this paper</span></span></span> indexed by <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e\in\{1,\ldots,E\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>E</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e\in\{1,\ldots,E\}</annotation></semantics></math>, and each party keeps its identity across episodes while the negotiation problem itself changes.
Episode <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>e</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e</annotation></semantics></math> involves a set of issues <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{K}_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒦</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{K}_{e}</annotation></semantics></math>, where each issue <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k\in\mathcal{K}_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒦</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k\in\mathcal{K}_{e}</annotation></semantics></math> has a finite set of options <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}_{e,k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}_{e,k}</annotation></semantics></math>.
A deal <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x\in\mathcal{X}_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x\in\mathcal{X}_{e}</annotation></semantics></math> assigns one option to every issue.
Each party <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> has a private score <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{i,k}^{e}(o)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mi>e</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>o</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{i,k}^{e}(o)</annotation></semantics></math> for each option and a private threshold <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta_{i}^{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>β</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>e</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{i}^{e}</annotation></semantics></math>, its best alternative to a negotiated agreement (BATNA).
The space of deals and party <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>’s additive utility are:</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{X}_{e}=\!\!\prod_{k\in\mathcal{K}_{e}}\mathcal{O}_{e,k},\quad u_{i}^{e}(x)=\!\!\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}_{e}}s_{i,k}^{e}(x_{k}),\quad x\in\mathcal{X}_{e}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mpadded style="width:0.716em;" width="0.716em"><mo>=</mo></mpadded><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∏</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒦</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></mrow></munder><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>e</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mpadded style="width:0.716em;" width="0.716em"><mo>=</mo></mpadded><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒦</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></mrow></munder><mrow><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mi>e</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{X}_{e}=\!\!\prod_{k\in\mathcal{K}_{e}}\mathcal{O}_{e,k},\quad u_{i}^{e}(x)=\!\!\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}_{e}}s_{i,k}^{e}(x_{k}),\quad x\in\mathcal{X}_{e}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">If the parties agree on a deal <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>, party <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> receives <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{i}^{e}(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>e</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{i}^{e}(x)</annotation></semantics></math>; otherwise, it receives <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta_{i}^{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>β</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>e</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{i}^{e}</annotation></semantics></math>.
The episode description and the party identities are public, while scores, BATNAs, and role instructions are private.
Each party also receives a qualitative description of what the others are likely to care about.
Honest parties want to reach an agreement, though they may differ in how readily they compromise.
Let <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{B}\subsetneq\mathcal{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><mo>⊊</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{B}\subsetneq\mathcal{N}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the adversarial parties, whose objective is to prevent an agreement.
Since this objective is private, honest parties cannot directly determine whether a rejection reflects sabotage or simply a demanding but honest counterpart.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>LLM Interaction and Agreement Protocol</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">An episode lasts at most <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{e}</annotation></semantics></math> rounds.
Parties propose in turn: in each round <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math>, the proposer <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{e,r}\in\mathcal{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{e,r}\in\mathcal{N}</annotation></semantics></math> submits a complete deal <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{e,r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{e,r}</annotation></semantics></math> with a public rationale, and every other party casts a binary vote <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{i,e,r}\in\{0,1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{i,e,r}\in\{0,1\}</annotation></semantics></math> with its own public rationale.
Let <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{C}_{i}^{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>e</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{C}_{i}^{e}</annotation></semantics></math> be party <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>’s initial context for episode <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>e</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e</annotation></semantics></math>, which contains the shared problem description, its private preferences and role, and the negotiation rules.
Let <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{e}</annotation></semantics></math> be the complete public transcript of episode <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>e</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e</annotation></semantics></math>, in which each round records the proposer, the proposed deal, the public rationales, the votes, and the outcome.
Let <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{H}_{e,r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>H</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{H}_{e,r}</annotation></semantics></math> be the history available in round <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math>, containing the <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> most recent completed rounds of <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{e}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Let <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{i,e,r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{i,e,r}</annotation></semantics></math> be the instruction for the current action; for a voter, it also includes the current deal and its rationale.
Finally, let <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m16" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\tau_{i\cdot}^{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0.222em">⋅</mo></mrow></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>e</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{i\cdot}^{e}</annotation></semantics></math> be party <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>’s private trust vector, defined below.
A model call in round <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> is:</p>
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathsf{Out}_{i,e,r}=\mathrm{LLM}\!\left(\mathcal{C}_{i}^{e},\,\bar{H}_{e,r},\,D_{i,e,r};\,\tau_{i\cdot}^{e}\right)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝖮𝗎𝗍</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mpadded style="width:2.270em;" width="2.270em"><mi>LLM</mi></mpadded><mrow><mo>(</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>e</mi></msubsup><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>H</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><mo rspace="0.337em">;</mo><msubsup><mi>τ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0.222em">⋅</mo></mrow><mi>e</mi></msubsup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathsf{Out}_{i,e,r}=\mathrm{LLM}\!\left(\mathcal{C}_{i}^{e},\,\bar{H}_{e,r},\,D_{i,e,r};\,\tau_{i\cdot}^{e}\right),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m19" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\tau_{i\cdot}^{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0.222em">⋅</mo></mrow></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>e</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{i\cdot}^{e}</annotation></semantics></math> is omitted for trust-agnostic agents.
Each output contains an action (deal or vote), a public rationale, and private reasoning (scratchpad).
Only the action and the rationale enter the public transcript.
All voters in a round see the same history and the same deal, but not each other’s votes.
A deal passes if at least <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n-1</annotation></semantics></math> parties accept it, where the proposer counts as accepting its own deal.
The first accepted deal becomes the final agreement <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{e,r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{e,r}</annotation></semantics></math> and ends the episode; if no deal passes within <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{e}</annotation></semantics></math> rounds, the episode ends in disagreement.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Trust as cross-episode state.</span>  

For each ordered pair <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i\neq j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>≠</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i\neq j</annotation></semantics></math>, the entry <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{ij}^{e}\in[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>τ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mi>e</mi></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{ij}^{e}\in[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math> is party <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>’s private trust in party <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math> at the start of episode <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>e</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e</annotation></semantics></math>, so <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\tau_{i\cdot}^{e}=(\tau_{ij}^{e})_{j\neq i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>τ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0.222em">⋅</mo></mrow><mi>e</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>τ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mi>e</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>≠</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{i\cdot}^{e}=(\tau_{ij}^{e})_{j\neq i}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Trust is directed and subjective: <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{ij}^{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>τ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mi>e</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{ij}^{e}</annotation></semantics></math> need not equal <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{ji}^{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>τ</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><mi>e</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{ji}^{e}</annotation></semantics></math>.
All entries start from prior <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{ij}^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>τ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{ij}^{1}</annotation></semantics></math> and remain fixed within each episode.
Raw negotiation transcripts do not cross episode boundaries, so the trust vector is the only state through which one negotiation can inform a later one.
Trust-aware agents maintain this vector and receive it as an explicit input to their decisions, as in Eq. (<a href="#S3.E2" title="In 3.2 LLM Interaction and Agreement Protocol ‣ 3 Problem Formulation ‣ Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust–Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>); trust-agnostic agents receive an otherwise identical context that includes neither the vector nor any mention of trust.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Trust–Agreement Gap</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Accurate trust improves outcomes only if agents act on it.
We therefore describe a trust-aware condition by two components.
The <em id="S3.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">assessment method</em> <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math> maps <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{e}</annotation></semantics></math> to updated trust.
The <em id="S3.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">decision policy</em> <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi=(m,I)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>I</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi=(m,I)</annotation></semantics></math> of the honest parties consists of the model <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> and an instruction <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>I</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I</annotation></semantics></math> specifying how trust should be used in decision making, with <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I=\varnothing" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∅</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I=\varnothing</annotation></semantics></math> when no such instruction is provided;
<math id="S3.SS3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math> maps the inputs in Eq. (<a href="#S3.E2" title="In 3.2 LLM Interaction and Agreement Protocol ‣ 3 Problem Formulation ‣ Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust–Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) to a deal or a vote.
The policy of the adversarial parties is held fixed.
Let <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha(\phi,\pi)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha(\phi,\pi)</annotation></semantics></math> be the probability that an episode ends in agreement when the honest parties follow <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math> and update trust with <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math>.
For a policy <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi^{\prime}=(m,I^{\prime})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>π</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>I</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi^{\prime}=(m,I^{\prime})</annotation></semantics></math> with the same model and any trust instruction <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>I</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math>, let <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{\pi}(\phi,\pi^{\prime})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>α</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>π</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha_{\pi}(\phi,\pi^{\prime})</annotation></semantics></math> be the probability of agreement when the honest parties follow <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>π</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math> but receive in every episode the trust that <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math> forms under <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math>.
Since trust is the only information carried across episodes, <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{\pi}(\phi,\pi)=\alpha(\phi,\pi)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>α</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha_{\pi}(\phi,\pi)=\alpha(\phi,\pi)</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmdefinition1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_definition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmdefinition1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Definition 1</span></span><span id="Thmdefinition1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Trust–agreement gap)<span id="Thmdefinition1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmdefinition1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Thmdefinition1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The trust–agreement gap of <math id="Thmdefinition1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi=(m,I)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>I</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi=(m,I)</annotation></semantics></math> is the agreement probability lost by not using its available trust as effectively as possible; that is, the difference between the highest agreement probability attainable by <math id="Thmdefinition1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> with the trust that <math id="Thmdefinition1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math> forms under <math id="Thmdefinition1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math> and the agreement probability under <math id="Thmdefinition1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{\mathrm{TA}}(\phi,\pi)=\sup_{I^{\prime}}\alpha_{\pi}\bigl(\phi,(m,I^{\prime})\bigr)-\alpha(\phi,\pi)\;\geq\;0," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>TA</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.1389em">=</mo><mrow><mrow><munder><mo lspace="0.1389em" movablelimits="false" rspace="0.167em">sup</mo><msup><mi>I</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></munder><mrow><msub><mi>α</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>I</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>π</mi><mo rspace="0.280em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mn> 0</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{\mathrm{TA}}(\phi,\pi)=\sup_{I^{\prime}}\alpha_{\pi}\bigl(\phi,(m,I^{\prime})\bigr)-\alpha(\phi,\pi)\;\geq\;0,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="Thmdefinition1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where the supremum (least upper bound) is taken over all trust instructions <math id="Thmdefinition1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>I</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Because the model and the trust are fixed and only the trust instruction varies, the gap isolates how well the model uses its trust, not how well it negotiates in general.
Dividing it by <math id="Thmdefinition1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1-\alpha(\phi,\pi)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1-\alpha(\phi,\pi)</annotation></semantics></math> gives the <em id="Thmdefinition1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">normalized gap</em> <math id="Thmdefinition1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta_{\mathrm{TA}}(\phi,\pi)\in[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi>TA</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta_{\mathrm{TA}}(\phi,\pi)\in[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="Thmdefinition1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha(\phi,\pi)&lt;1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha(\phi,\pi)&lt;1</annotation></semantics></math>, the share of disagreements that better use of the same trust could avoid.</p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We cannot compute the supremum, but any evaluated policy <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi^{\prime}=(m,I^{\prime})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>π</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>I</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi^{\prime}=(m,I^{\prime})</annotation></semantics></math> bounds the gap from below:</p>
<table id="S3.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{\pi}(\phi,\pi^{\prime})-\alpha(\phi,\pi)\;\leq\;\Delta_{\mathrm{TA}}(\phi,\pi)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>α</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>π</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>π</mi><mo rspace="0.280em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.558em">≤</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>TA</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha_{\pi}(\phi,\pi^{\prime})-\alpha(\phi,\pi)\;\leq\;\Delta_{\mathrm{TA}}(\phi,\pi).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.2" class="ltx_p">Dividing both sides by <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1-\alpha(\phi,\pi)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1-\alpha(\phi,\pi)</annotation></semantics></math> bounds the normalized gap <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta_{\mathrm{TA}}(\phi,\pi)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi>TA</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta_{\mathrm{TA}}(\phi,\pi)</annotation></semantics></math> from below in the same way.
A positive lower bound therefore shows that the same model, given the same trust, reaches agreement more often under a different instruction, so part of the value of its trust is left unused.
A lower bound near zero reveals no gap, but it does not show that none exists.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>The <span id="S4.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">TASMAN</span> Framework</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">TASMAN</span> is a repeated multi-party negotiation framework that implements the game of Section <a href="#S3" title="3 Problem Formulation ‣ Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust–Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> with LLM agents whose trust carries over between episodes and explicitly informs their decisions.
In each episode, agents negotiate according to their roles; after the episode, each agent assesses its counterparts from the public transcript and updates its trust.
We first describe how agents assess trust and then how they use it in their decisions.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Trust Assessment</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">After each episode, every agent assesses its counterparts with one of the following three methods, which give the LLM increasing control over the trust computation: the <em id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">beta reputation system</em> (BRS), <em id="S4.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">rubric-based</em> assessment, and <em id="S4.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">free-form</em> assessment.
In all three methods, the agent receives its episode context, its current trust vector, the assessment instructions, and the complete public transcript <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{e}</annotation></semantics></math> of episode <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>e</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e</annotation></semantics></math>.
In the rubric-based and free-form methods, the agent produces an episode trust signal <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{ij}^{e}\in[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mi>e</mi></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{ij}^{e}\in[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math> for each counterpart <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math>, with higher values for behavior it judges more trustworthy, and updates its trust as an exponential moving average (EMA),</p>
<table id="S4.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{ij}^{e+1}=\lambda\,\tau_{ij}^{e}+(1-\lambda)\,z_{ij}^{e}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>τ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>τ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mi>e</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>λ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mi>e</mi></msubsup></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{ij}^{e+1}=\lambda\,\tau_{ij}^{e}+(1-\lambda)\,z_{ij}^{e},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda\in[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda\in[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math> controls how strongly past experience persists.
LLM computes this update itself and reports the result.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Beta reputation system (BRS).</span>  
We adapt the beta reputation system <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite> to LLM agents, so that the LLM supplies evidence and a Bayesian update rule computes trust.
After each episode, the agent reports the number of positive and negative observations for each counterpart, such as a compromise that another party confirms or a reversal of an explicit endorsement without explanation.
The system adds these counts, normalized per episode, to past evidence discounted by a forgetting factor of <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math>, and sets trust to the mean of the resulting Beta distribution with a uniform prior.
Agents retrieve their updated scores through a read-only tool; Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Beta Reputation System (BRS) ‣ Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust–Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a> describes the feedback criteria and the update rule in detail.
Appendix <a href="#A6.SS7" title="F.7 BRS Feedback Prompt ‣ Appendix F Prompts ‣ Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust–Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.7</span></a> provides the feedback prompt.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Rubric-based trust (Rubric).</span>  
The agent computes <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{ij}^{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mi>e</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{ij}^{e}</annotation></semantics></math> from a rubric of five behavioral metrics calculated from public information.
The metrics draw on work on behavioral consistency, causal responsibility, strategic manipulation, reputation, and trust aggregation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>, <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>, <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>, <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>, <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>, <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite>; Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Rubric-Based Trust ‣ Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust–Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a> gives our operational definitions, and Appendix <a href="#A2.SS7" title="B.7 Connection to Prior Work ‣ Appendix B Rubric-Based Trust ‣ Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust–Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.7</span></a> describes these connections.
For each round <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> of episode <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>e</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e</annotation></semantics></math>, let <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{r}</annotation></semantics></math> be its number of rejections, and let <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>q</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> be the minimum number of rejections that fails a proposal.</p>
<ul id="S4.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Counterfactual blame.</em>
<math id="S4.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b(j)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b(j)</annotation></semantics></math> is the fraction of decisive rounds <math id="S4.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{d}}_{j}=\{r:p_{e,r}\neq j,\ q_{r}=q^{*}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>d</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><mo>≠</mo><mi>j</mi><mo rspace="0.667em">,</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>q</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{d}}_{j}=\{r:p_{e,r}\neq j,\ q_{r}=q^{*}\}</annotation></semantics></math> in which <math id="S4.I1.i1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math> rejected, i.e., <math id="S4.I1.i1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b(j)=\tfrac{1}{|\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{d}}_{j}|}\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{d}}_{j}}(1-v_{j,e,r})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>d</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>∈</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>d</mi></msubsup></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b(j)=\tfrac{1}{|\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{d}}_{j}|}\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{d}}_{j}}(1-v_{j,e,r})</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Cooperation as proposer.</em>
<math id="S4.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C(j)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C(j)</annotation></semantics></math> is the acceptance fraction of <math id="S4.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math>’s deals, averaged over the rounds with <math id="S4.I1.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{e,r}=j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{e,r}=j</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Outlier rejection rate.</em>
<math id="S4.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(j)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(j)</annotation></semantics></math> is the fraction of <math id="S4.I1.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math>’s votes in which <math id="S4.I1.i3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math> rejects while the remaining voters reject fewer than <math id="S4.I1.i3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>q</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>, rejections the rest of the group does not share.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S4.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Targeted-failure rate.</em>
<math id="S4.I1.i4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T(j)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T(j)</annotation></semantics></math> is the fraction of <math id="S4.I1.i4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math>’s proposals that failed with exactly <math id="S4.I1.i4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>q</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> rejections, identifying deals repeatedly placed at the failure boundary.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S4.I1.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Vote–priority inconsistency.</em>
<math id="S4.I1.i5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F(j)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F(j)</annotation></semantics></math> is the fraction of <math id="S4.I1.i5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math>’s votes whose direction contradicts <math id="S4.I1.i5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math>’s public rationales and priorities.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Metrics with too little evidence take default values: <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b(j)=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b(j)=0</annotation></semantics></math> when <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{d}}_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>d</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{d}}_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> is empty, <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T(j)=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T(j)=0</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C(j)=0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C(j)=0.5</annotation></semantics></math> when <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math> never proposed, and <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(j)=F(j)=0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(j)=F(j)=0.5</annotation></semantics></math> when <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math> cast fewer than three non-proposer votes to evaluate. The agent then chooses <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{1},\ldots,w_{5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>5</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{1},\ldots,w_{5}</annotation></semantics></math>, nonnegative weights that sum to one, applies them uniformly across counterparts, and combines the metrics into an obstruction score:</p>
<table id="S4.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{Obs}_{ij}^{e}=w_{1}b(j)+w_{2}\,\bigl[1-C(j)\bigr]+w_{3}O(j)+w_{4}T(j)+w_{5}F(j)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>Obs</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mi>e</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">[</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>O</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>F</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{Obs}_{ij}^{e}=w_{1}b(j)+w_{2}\,\bigl[1-C(j)\bigr]+w_{3}O(j)+w_{4}T(j)+w_{5}F(j).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS1.p4.2" class="ltx_p">The episode signal is <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{ij}^{e}=1-\mathrm{Obs}_{ij}^{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mi>e</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>Obs</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mi>e</mi></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{ij}^{e}=1-\mathrm{Obs}_{ij}^{e}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Appendix <a href="#A6.SS8" title="F.8 Rubric-based Trust-Update Prompt ‣ Appendix F Prompts ‣ Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust–Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.8</span></a> provides the rubric-based trust update prompt.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Free-form trust (FF).</span>  
The agent receives no rubric: it decides which aspects of <math id="S4.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{e}</annotation></semantics></math> are informative and which criteria to use, describes the evidence it relies on, and reports <math id="S4.SS1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{ij}^{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mi>e</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{ij}^{e}</annotation></semantics></math> directly.
Section <a href="#S5.SS6" title="5.6 Free-form Criteria and Declared Weights ‣ 5 Experiments and Results ‣ Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust–Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.6</span></a> examines the LLM reported criteria and their weights.
Appendix <a href="#A6.SS9" title="F.9 Free-Form Trust-Update Prompt ‣ Appendix F Prompts ‣ Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust–Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.9</span></a> provides the free-form trust update prompt.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
