<section id="S5.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.4 </span>Trust–Agreement Gap</h3>

<div id="S5.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S5.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Agents form accurate trust but leave much of its value unused.</em>
Across the trust-aware conditions, honest agents form accurate trust (Section <a href="#S5.SS2" title="5.2 Trust Formation ‣ 5 Experiments and Results ‣ Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust–Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.2</span></a>), yet with <math id="S5.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math>, no condition raises agreement significantly over no trust (Table <a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 5.2 Trust Formation ‣ 5 Experiments and Results ‣ Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust–Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>).
The disagreement rate is <math id="S5.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="47.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>47.0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">47.0</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S5.SS4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="64.5\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>64.5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">64.5\%</annotation></semantics></math> across models, settings, and assessment methods, although every episode contains a deal that meets all honest parties’ BATNAs and that they could pass without the adversary’s vote.
For <span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">grok-r</span> in 1HB+3G, the same trust raises agreement by <math id="S5.SS4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{S\to P}=16.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>16.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{S\to P}=16.5</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S5.SS4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="30.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>30.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30.5</annotation></semantics></math> points once agents are guided to use it, and all three paired intervals exclude zero (Table <a href="#S5.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 5.3 Negotiation Outcomes ‣ 5 Experiments and Results ‣ Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust–Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>).
In this setting, the <math id="S5.SS4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math> trust detects the adversary in at least <math id="S5.SS4.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="91\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>91</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">91\%</annotation></semantics></math> of assessments, yet <math id="S5.SS4.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta_{S\to P}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>δ</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta_{S\to P}</annotation></semantics></math> shows that better use of it could avoid at least <math id="S5.SS4.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="30" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>30</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S5.SS4.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="47\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>47</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">47\%</annotation></semantics></math> of the <math id="S5.SS4.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math> disagreements.
BRS, which has the lowest <math id="S5.SS4.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math> agreement (<math id="S5.SS4.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="35.5\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>35.5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">35.5\%</annotation></semantics></math>), has the largest lower bound.
In 2HB+2G, <span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">grok-r</span>’s lower bounds (<math id="S5.SS4.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.5</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S5.SS4.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>8.0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8.0</annotation></semantics></math> points) are positive, but their intervals include zero.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S5.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">The gains come from how agents use trust, not from better trust.</em>
<math id="S5.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S{+}P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S{+}P</annotation></semantics></math> changes both how agents use trust and the trust they form.
The <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S{\to}P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S{\to}P</annotation></semantics></math> condition separates the two: with the trust formed under <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math>, guidance alone raises <span id="S5.SS4.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">grok-r</span>’s agreement in 1HB+3G by <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{S\to P}=25.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>25.0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{S\to P}=25.0</annotation></semantics></math> points on average, close to the <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="25.8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>25.8</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">25.8</annotation></semantics></math>-point average of <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{S+P}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{S+P}</annotation></semantics></math> (Table <a href="#S5.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 5.3 Negotiation Outcomes ‣ 5 Experiments and Results ‣ Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust–Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>).
The remaining effect of better trust, <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{\mathrm{trust}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>trust</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{\mathrm{trust}}</annotation></semantics></math>, ranges from <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-7.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>7.0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-7.0</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="7.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>7.0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">7.0</annotation></semantics></math> points, and no interval excludes zero.
This holds even where <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S{+}P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S{+}P</annotation></semantics></math> forms clearly better trust: <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{\mathrm{trust}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>trust</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{\mathrm{trust}}</annotation></semantics></math> is <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.5</annotation></semantics></math> points for free-form assessment in 2HB+2G, where detection rises from <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="75.1\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>75.1</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">75.1\%</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="89.2\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>89.2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">89.2\%</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-7.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>7.0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-7.0</annotation></semantics></math> points for rubric-based assessment in 1HB+3G, where it rises from <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="93.1\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>93.1</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">93.1\%</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="98.1\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>98.1</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">98.1\%</annotation></semantics></math>.
Accurate trust is thus necessary but not sufficient; its value depends on how the model uses it.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S5.SS4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">With the same trust, guidance changes how agents vote.</em>
Under <math id="S5.SS4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S{\to}P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S{\to}P</annotation></semantics></math>, hard bargainers reject <math id="S5.SS4.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4.2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4.2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4.2</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S5.SS4.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8.3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>8.3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8.3</annotation></semantics></math> points fewer of the proposals that clear their BATNA than under <math id="S5.SS4.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math>, and the conversion of honest-feasible proposals rises by <math id="S5.SS4.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3.8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3.8</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.8</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S5.SS4.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="14.6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>14.6</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">14.6</annotation></semantics></math> points.
All twelve paired intervals exclude zero, including those in 2HB+2G.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S5.SS4.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">The unused value depends on informative trust.</em>
Under the same guidance, <span id="S5.SS4.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">grok-r</span>’s <math id="S5.SS4.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S{\to}P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S{\to}P</annotation></semantics></math> exceeds its <math id="S5.SS4.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{0.5}{+}P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0.5</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{0.5}{+}P</annotation></semantics></math> (Table <a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 5.2 Trust Formation ‣ 5 Experiments and Results ‣ Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust–Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) by <math id="S5.SS4.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="12.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>12.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">12.5</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S5.SS4.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="17.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>17.0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">17.0</annotation></semantics></math> points of agreement in all six conditions, and every paired interval excludes zero.
The gap therefore reflects what the trust reveals about the adversary, not the instruction alone.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S5.SS4.p5.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">S+P reveals no gap for <span id="S5.SS4.p5.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gemini-r</span>.</em>
For <span id="S5.SS4.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gemini-r</span>, <math id="S5.SS4.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{S+P}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{S+P}</annotation></semantics></math> lies between <math id="S5.SS4.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-3.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-3.5</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.SS4.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4.0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4.0</annotation></semantics></math> points (Table <a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 5.2 Trust Formation ‣ 5 Experiments and Results ‣ Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust–Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>), and <math id="S5.SS4.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.SS4.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S{+}P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S{+}P</annotation></semantics></math> do not differ significantly under any method.
This does not show that <span id="S5.SS4.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gemini-r</span> uses its trust fully, only that <math id="S5.SS4.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S{+}P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S{+}P</annotation></semantics></math> does not improve its trust use.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.5 </span>Trust and Voting Behavior</h3>

<div id="S5.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S5.SS5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Agents withhold acceptance from proposers they distrust.</em>
Figure <a href="#S5.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 5.5 Trust and Voting Behavior ‣ 5 Experiments and Results ‣ Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust–Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> includes only offers that clear the voter’s BATNA, so each rejection is a strategic holdout.
In every condition, agents accept high-trust proposers more often than low-trust ones, by <math id="S5.SS5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="9.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>9.0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">9.0</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S5.SS5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="39.9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>39.9</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">39.9</annotation></semantics></math> points on average.
High-trust acceptance stays within <math id="S5.SS5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="46.2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>46.2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">46.2</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S5.SS5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="58.4\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>58.4</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">58.4\%</annotation></semantics></math>, while low-trust acceptance varies more widely (<math id="S5.SS5.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="18.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>18.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">18.5</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S5.SS5.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="42.2\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>42.2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">42.2\%</annotation></semantics></math>).
Because detection is high, <math id="S5.SS5.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="69" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>69</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">69</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S5.SS5.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="100\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>100</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100\%</annotation></semantics></math> of low-trust votes concern the adversary’s proposals, except <span id="S5.SS5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gemini-r</span>’s rubric-based assessment, where only <math id="S5.SS5.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="27" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>27</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">27</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S5.SS5.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="30\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>30</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30\%</annotation></semantics></math> do and most target honest hard bargainers.
Overall, agents accept the adversary’s proposals in only <math id="S5.SS5.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="15.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>15.0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">15.0</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S5.SS5.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="28.2\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>28.2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">28.2\%</annotation></semantics></math> of their votes, compared with <math id="S5.SS5.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="47.7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>47.7</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">47.7</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S5.SS5.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="60.4\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>60.4</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">60.4\%</annotation></semantics></math> for honest proposals.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.31971v1/fig_trust_conditioned_acceptance_column_brs.svg" id="S5.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:286/137;" width="286" height="137"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span><span id="S5.F3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Honest parties’ acceptance rate of a proposal when their trust in the proposer is low (<math id="S5.F3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&lt;0.45" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.45</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&lt;0.45</annotation></semantics></math>) or high (<math id="S5.F3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&gt;0.55" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0.55</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&gt;0.55</annotation></semantics></math>)</span>; the neutral band is excluded. Error bars are 95% CI. The results for other models are in Appendix <a href="#A5.SS4" title="E.4 Trust and Voting Behavior ‣ Appendix E Additional Quantitative Results ‣ Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust–Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.4</span></a>.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S5.SS5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">S+P strengthens the voting response only for <span id="S5.SS5.p2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">grok-r</span>.</em>
For <span id="S5.SS5.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">grok-r</span>, <math id="S5.SS5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S{+}P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S{+}P</annotation></semantics></math> widens the acceptance gap under every method by <math id="S5.SS5.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="9.2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>9.2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">9.2</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S5.SS5.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="26.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>26.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">26.5</annotation></semantics></math> points, most under free-form.
It also raises <span id="S5.SS5.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">grok-r</span>’s acceptance of high-trust proposers by <math id="S5.SS5.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="7.2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>7.2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">7.2</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S5.SS5.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="12.2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>12.2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">12.2</annotation></semantics></math> points, consistent with the drop in hard-bargainer rejections under both <math id="S5.SS5.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S{+}P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S{+}P</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.SS5.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S{\to}P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S{\to}P</annotation></semantics></math> (Sections <a href="#S5.SS3" title="5.3 Negotiation Outcomes ‣ 5 Experiments and Results ‣ Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust–Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.3</span></a> and <a href="#S5.SS4" title="5.4 Trust–Agreement Gap ‣ 5 Experiments and Results ‣ Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust–Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.4</span></a>).
For <span id="S5.SS5.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gemini-r</span>, <math id="S5.SS5.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S{+}P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S{+}P</annotation></semantics></math> changes the gap by at most <math id="S5.SS5.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.1</annotation></semantics></math> points, consistent with its near-zero <math id="S5.SS5.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{S+P}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{S+P}</annotation></semantics></math> (Section <a href="#S5.SS4" title="5.4 Trust–Agreement Gap ‣ 5 Experiments and Results ‣ Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust–Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.4</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F4" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.31971v1/fig_freeform_criteria_main.svg" id="S5.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:429/154;" width="429" height="154"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span><span id="S5.F4.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Declared free-form trust criteria (2HB+2G).</span> Each bar shows the mean share of declared weight that honest assessors give each category under <math id="S5.F4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math> or <math id="S5.F4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S{+}P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S{+}P</annotation></semantics></math>. Appendix <a href="#A4.SS1" title="D.1 Consistency and Compromise Receive the Largest Weights ‣ Appendix D Free-Form Trust Criteria and Declared Weights ‣ Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust–Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.1</span></a> reports all six models.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.6 </span>Free-form Criteria and Declared Weights</h3>

<div id="S5.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">After each free-form assessment, the agent names the criteria it used and their approximate weights, with one weight vector for all counterparts.
We group the criteria into eight behavioral categories and an <em id="S5.SS6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Other</em> category, normalize each weight vector, and average over honest agents, episodes, and trajectories.
Agents name approximately four criteria per assessment on average.
Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Free-Form Trust Criteria and Declared Weights ‣ Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust–Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a> gives a detailed analysis of reported criteria of all six models.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS6.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS6.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S5.SS6.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Agents judge trust mainly by consistency and compromise.</em>
Consistency with stated priorities and willingness to compromise together receive <math id="S5.SS6.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="73" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>73</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">73</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S5.SS6.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="77\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>77</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">77\%</annotation></semantics></math> of the declared weight across models (Figure <a href="#S5.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 5.5 Trust and Voting Behavior ‣ 5 Experiments and Results ‣ Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust–Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>).
Constructive proposals receive <math id="S5.SS6.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>8</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S5.SS6.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="11\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>11</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">11\%</annotation></semantics></math>, and obstruction receives at most <math id="S5.SS6.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3.3\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3.3</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.3\%</annotation></semantics></math>.
Thus, when the LLM chooses its own criteria, it rewards cooperative behavior rather than penalizing rejections.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS6.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS6.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S5.SS6.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">The two models weigh these criteria differently, and guidance narrows the difference.</em>
<span id="S5.SS6.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">grok-r</span> gives consistency <math id="S5.SS6.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="53.0\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>53.0</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">53.0\%</annotation></semantics></math> of its weight under <math id="S5.SS6.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.SS6.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="50.1\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>50.1</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50.1\%</annotation></semantics></math> under <math id="S5.SS6.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S{+}P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S{+}P</annotation></semantics></math>, compared with <math id="S5.SS6.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="38.2\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>38.2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">38.2\%</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.SS6.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="44.8\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>44.8</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">44.8\%</annotation></semantics></math> for <span id="S5.SS6.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gemini-r</span>.
<span id="S5.SS6.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gemini-r</span> instead gives more weight to compromise (<math id="S5.SS6.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="34.7\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>34.7</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">34.7\%</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.SS6.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="31.8\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>31.8</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">31.8\%</annotation></semantics></math>, compared with <math id="S5.SS6.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="21.5\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>21.5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">21.5\%</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.SS6.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="26.4\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>26.4</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">26.4\%</annotation></semantics></math>).
Under <math id="S5.SS6.p3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S{+}P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S{+}P</annotation></semantics></math>, the gap between the models shrinks from <math id="S5.SS6.p3.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="14.8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>14.8</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">14.8</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S5.SS6.p3.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5.3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>5.3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5.3</annotation></semantics></math> points for consistency and from <math id="S5.SS6.p3.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="13.2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>13.2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">13.2</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S5.SS6.p3.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5.4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>5.4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5.4</annotation></semantics></math> points for compromise.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS6.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS6.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S5.SS6.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Agents revise their criteria from episode to episode.</em>
An agent’s allocation across categories changes between consecutive episodes in <math id="S5.SS6.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="98.3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>98.3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">98.3</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S5.SS6.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="99.1\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>99.1</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">99.1\%</annotation></semantics></math> of cases, and on average <math id="S5.SS6.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="29" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>29</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">29</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S5.SS6.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="34\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>34</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">34\%</annotation></semantics></math> of its weight moves to different categories.
Unlike the rubric-based trust, the criteria therefore adapt to what the agent observed in each episode.
This flexibility also makes free-form trust depend on the model’s own judgment, consistent with the model-dependent results in Section <a href="#S5.SS2" title="5.2 Trust Formation ‣ 5 Experiments and Results ‣ Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust–Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>

<span id="S5.T4.5.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left"><span id="S5.T4.5.1.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evidence from the agents’ reasoning</span></span>

<tr id="S5.T4.5.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S5.T4.5.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:5.0pt;padding-right:5.0pt;">
<span id="S5.T4.5.2.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block" style="width:119.0pt;">
<span id="S5.T4.5.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left">
<span id="S5.T4.5.2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_top" style="width:345.0pt;">
<span id="S5.T4.5.2.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.T4.5.2.1.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="position:relative; bottom:-1.5pt;">
<span id="S5.T4.5.2.1.1.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_top" style="width:342.0pt;--ltx-bg-color:#EDEDED;">
<span id="S5.T4.5.2.1.1.1.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left"><em id="S5.T4.5.2.1.1.1.1.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Finding 1. Knowing whom to trust is not enough.</em></span>
</span></span></span>
<span id="S5.T4.5.2.1.1.1.1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.T4.5.2.1.1.1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Near misses.</span> A deal that every honest party could accept fails because one of them rejects it together with the adversary, despite trusting the proposer.</span>
</span></span>
</span></td>
<td id="S5.T4.5.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:5.0pt;padding-right:5.0pt;">
<span id="S5.T4.5.2.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block">

The <span id="S5.T4.p4.pic2.1.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">low trust</span> for CASB makes this deal objectively bad for me.”</em></span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>

</span></span></span>
<span id="S5.T4.5.6.1.1.1.1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.T4.5.6.1.1.1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Coalition formation.</span> A deal survives one rejection, so proposers write off the low-trust agent’s vote.</span>

</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S5.T4.p5.pic2" class="ltx_picture" height="38.69" overflow="visible" style="vertical-align:-38.69px" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 236.61 38.69" width="236.61"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,38.69) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#F6EFF5;" fill="#F6EFF5" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 2.08 L 0 36.62 C 0 37.76 0.93 38.69 2.08 38.69 L 234.54 38.69 C 235.68 38.69 236.61 37.76 236.61 36.62 L 236.61 2.08 C 236.61 0.93 235.68 0 234.54 0 L 2.08 0 C 0.93 0 0 0.93 0 2.08 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#8C3B7E;--ltx-fill-color:#8C3B7E;--ltx-fg-color:#8C3B7E;" color="#8C3B7E" fill="#8C3B7E" stroke="#8C3B7E" stroke-dasharray="2.6pt,1.9pt" stroke-dashoffset="0.0pt" stroke-width="0.9pt"><path style="fill:none" d="M 0.62 2.08 L 0.62 36.62 C 0.62 37.42 1.27 38.07 2.08 38.07 L 234.54 38.07 C 235.34 38.07 235.99 37.42 235.99 36.62 L 235.99 2.08 C 235.99 1.27 235.34 0.62 234.54 0.62 L 2.08 0.62 C 1.27 0.62 0.62 1.27 0.62 2.08 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 8.09 4.43)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:15.93em;--ltx-fo-height:2.36em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.2em;font-size:10pt;" height="35.37" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 32.6)" width="220.43"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">

</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</span></span></span></span>

</span></span>
</span></td>

<section id="S5.SS7" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.7 </span>Behavior Analysis</h3>

<div id="S5.SS7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To understand how trust changes the agents’ reasoning (RQ4), we compare the scratchpads of trust-aware and trust-agnostic agents (Table <a href="#S5.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 5.6 Free-form Criteria and Declared Weights ‣ 5 Experiments and Results ‣ Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust–Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS7.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS7.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S5.SS7.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Knowing whom to trust is not enough.</em>
Most failed episodes are near misses: an honest proposal that clears every honest BATNA fails because one hard bargainer rejects it together with the adversary.
In 2HB+2G, this occurs in around <math id="S5.SS7.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="90\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>90</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">90\%</annotation></semantics></math> of the failed <span id="S5.SS7.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gemini-r</span> episodes with trust and in up to <math id="S5.SS7.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="48\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>48</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">48\%</annotation></semantics></math> of the <span id="S5.SS7.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">grok-r</span> ones.
This deciding holdout usually detects the adversary but rarely sees that the adversary’s rejection makes its own vote decisive (<math id="S5.SS7.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.8\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.8</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.8\%</annotation></semantics></math> cases).
Agents thus identify the adversary but do not cast the vote that passes the deal, which is the trust–agreement gap of Section <a href="#S5.SS4" title="5.4 Trust–Agreement Gap ‣ 5 Experiments and Results ‣ Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust–Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.4</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS7.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS7.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S5.SS7.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Trust changes what agents reason about.</em>
Without trust, <math id="S5.SS7.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.5</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S5.SS7.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2.3\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2.3</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.3\%</annotation></semantics></math> of votes discuss the proposer’s credibility; with trust, <math id="S5.SS7.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="91" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>91</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">91</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S5.SS7.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="99\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>99</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">99\%</annotation></semantics></math> (<span id="S5.SS7.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">grok-r</span>) and <math id="S5.SS7.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="20" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>20</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">20</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S5.SS7.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="63\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>63</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">63\%</annotation></semantics></math> (<span id="S5.SS7.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gemini-r</span>) judge the proposer.
Low trust makes voters doubt the offers even when they clear the BATNA (<math id="S5.SS7.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="33" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>33</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">33</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S5.SS7.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="52\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>52</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">52\%</annotation></semantics></math>), but trust never makes them accept a below-BATNA offer.
So trust adds to utility-based reasoning rather than replacing it.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS7.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS7.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S5.SS7.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Trust changes strategic behavior.</em>
Since a deal survives one rejection, proposers increasingly build deals that pass without the low-trust adversary’s vote: <math id="S5.SS7.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S5.SS7.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="13\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>13</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">13\%</annotation></semantics></math> of coded proposals without trust, <math id="S5.SS7.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="19" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>19</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">19</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S5.SS7.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="37\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>37</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">37\%</annotation></semantics></math> under <math id="S5.SS7.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S5.SS7.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="41" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>41</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">41</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S5.SS7.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="52\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>52</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">52\%</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="S5.SS7.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S{+}P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S{+}P</annotation></semantics></math>.
Voters likewise hold out against low-trust proposers, mostly the adversary (Figure <a href="#S5.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 5.5 Trust and Voting Behavior ‣ 5 Experiments and Results ‣ Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust–Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS7.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS7.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S5.SS7.p5.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">S+P changes how the same trust is used.</em>
With the same trust as under <math id="S5.SS7.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.SS7.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S{\to}P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S{\to}P</annotation></semantics></math> makes <span id="S5.SS7.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">grok-r</span>’s hard bargainers accept <math id="S5.SS7.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="7.4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>7.4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">7.4</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S5.SS7.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="11.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>11.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">11.5</annotation></semantics></math> points more of the honest offers (2HB+2G).
When they settle, they more often argue that the adversary will keep blocking (<math id="S5.SS7.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="35\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>35</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">35\%</annotation></semantics></math> under <math id="S5.SS7.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.SS7.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="62\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>62</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">62\%</annotation></semantics></math> under <math id="S5.SS7.p5.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S{\to}P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S{\to}P</annotation></semantics></math>).
This shift underlies the positive <math id="S5.SS7.p5.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{S\to P}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{S\to P}</annotation></semantics></math> in Section <a href="#S5.SS4" title="5.4 Trust–Agreement Gap ‣ 5 Experiments and Results ‣ Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust–Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.4</span></a>.
<span id="S5.SS7.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gemini-r</span> instead ignores or sets aside its trust in <math id="S5.SS7.p5.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="74" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>74</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">74</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S5.SS7.p5.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="94\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>94</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">94\%</annotation></semantics></math> of its deciding holdouts (<math id="S5.SS7.p5.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>10</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S5.SS7.p5.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="16\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16\%</annotation></semantics></math> for <span id="S5.SS7.p5.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">grok-r</span>), so guidance does not strengthen its voting response (Section <a href="#S5.SS5" title="5.5 Trust and Voting Behavior ‣ 5 Experiments and Results ‣ Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust–Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.5</span></a>) and its more accurate trust brings smaller gains (Section <a href="#S5.SS3" title="5.3 Negotiation Outcomes ‣ 5 Experiments and Results ‣ Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust–Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.3</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">LLM agents will increasingly negotiate on behalf of individuals and organizations through repeated interactions with the same counterparts, some of whom may attempt to prevent agreement.
To investigate whether trust can improve outcomes in these interactions, we introduce <span id="S6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">TASMAN</span>, a repeated multi-party negotiation game framework in which agents maintain pairwise trust estimates that carry over across games with a covert adversary.
Our results show that trust-aware agents can identify the adversary within a few games.
While the best trust assessment method varies across models, our adaptation of BRS performs reliably across all evaluated conditions.
However, reliable trust estimates do not consistently translate into better agreements.
Without explicit guidance, LLMs cannot leverage trust to significantly improve their negotiation outcomes, and even with guidance, the gains depend on the model.
We capture this limitation through the trust–agreement gap and estimate a lower bound on the agreement rate lost when agents fail to use their available trust effectively.
These findings show that the benefits of trust depend not only on the accuracy of trust estimates but also on how agents incorporate them into their negotiation decisions.
Finally, our study considers a single adversary and agents that are prompted rather than trained to use trust.
Future work should examine multiple and adaptive adversaries and train agents to reduce this <em id="S6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">trust–agreement gap</em>.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Negotiation Scenario Generation</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This subsection describes how we created the 2HB+2G and 1HB+3G scenario sets. A <em id="A1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">scenario</em> specifies the public negotiation problem and each party’s
private scores and threshold. A <em id="A1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">game</em>, or <em id="A1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">episode</em>, is a
negotiation conducted under that scenario.
We call a package/deal <em id="A1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">honest-feasible</em> when it clears the
threshold of every honest party. This is a property of the scenario, regardless
of whether the agents find or accept the package during negotiation.</p>
</div>
<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>2HB+2G Scenario Set</h3>

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The main set contains two hard bargainers (SkyDrop and City Transport), two
general (Privacy Coalition and Couriers Guild), and one adversarial
party (Aviation Safety). These roles remain fixed across the twenty scenarios.
Each party has additive private scores with a maximum utility of 100, and each
honest threshold lies between 60 and 70.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The scores create disagreement without removing the possibility of agreement.
On one issue, the hard bargainers prefer different options, neither of which is
acceptable to all honest parties; a third option provides a compromise. A
second issue favors the two hard bargainers differently, while the remaining
issues give the general agents distinct attainable priorities. Consequently,
the hard bargainers must make concessions, but several agreements remain
available. Each scenario contains 8–10 honest-feasible packages.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The adversarial party receives a
plausible public preference profile, while its hidden objective is to prevent
agreement. The final set was generated with the fixed seed
<math id="A1.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="11000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>11000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">11000</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2 </span>1HB+3G Scenario Set</h3>

<div id="A1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the 1HB+3G set, SkyDrop is the hard bargainer and the other three honest
parties are general negotiators. The public
content matches the corresponding 2HB+2G scenario; only the private scores,
thresholds, roles, and preference descriptions differ.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">One issue requires the hard bargainer to accept a compromise. The remaining
issues vary which honest party must make the largest concession, and this
responsibility is distributed across the hard bargainer and the three general
agents. No honest party’s ideal package is honest-feasible, and each scenario
contains 7 or 8 honest-feasible packages. Thus, the smaller number of hard
bargainers does not make agreement automatic.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">As in the main set, the adversarial party receives plausible visible
preferences while its hidden objective is to prevent agreement. The final set
was generated with the fixed seed <math id="A1.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="31000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>31000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">31000</annotation></semantics></math>, and every experimental condition
uses the same scenario files.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.3 </span>Why the 1HB+3G Set Requires Different Private Scores</h3>

<div id="A1.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The 1HB+3G set tests whether the findings extend to a population with fewer
hard bargainers. Changing only the role label would not produce a suitable
comparison because the original scores were designed for two hard bargainers.
Since proposing a package also counts as accepting it, retaining those scores
with one hard bargainer could make agreement nearly automatic.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.T5" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 5: </span><span id="A1.T5.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Structural comparison of the two fixed scenario sets.</span> An ideal package gives an agent its highest-scoring option on every issue. Values aggregate all 20 scenarios; option changes and utility losses are role means. HB: hard bargainer, G: general agent.</figcaption>

<div id="A1.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We retained the public projects, parties, issues, options, and their order, but
generated new private scores and thresholds. The new scores preserve the need
for compromise while changing the role composition. Table <a href="#A1.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ A.3 Why the 1HB+3G Set Requires Different Private Scores ‣ Appendix A Negotiation Scenario Generation ‣ Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust–Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>
compares the two fixed sets; these values describe the scenarios rather than
the observed negotiation outcomes.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Because the private scores differ, comparisons between the two sets show
whether the findings extend to another role composition; they do not isolate
the effect of removing one hard bargainer. Within each set, all trust conditions
use identical scenarios and episode order, with randomization matched across
conditions.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Rubric-Based Trust</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Section 4.1 of the main paper summarizes rubric-based trust and the beta
reputation system (BRS). This appendix gives the complete definitions of the
five rubric metrics, describes how the agent combines them into a trust
update, and relates each metric to prior work. Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Beta Reputation System (BRS) ‣ Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust–Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a> then
describes our implementation of BRS.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Under rubric-based trust, every assessing agent computes an episode trust
signal from the same rubric of five behavioral metrics. After episode <math id="A2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>e</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e</annotation></semantics></math>,
the agent receives the complete public transcript <math id="A2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{e}</annotation></semantics></math>, which contains the
proposals, public rationales, votes, and outcomes of every completed round.
The transcript excludes the private reasoning and utility tables of other
agents. To evaluate vote–priority inconsistency, the assessor may also use
the qualitative description of each party’s priorities in its system template
(Appendix <a href="#A6.SS2" title="F.2 System Template ‣ Appendix F Prompts ‣ Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust–Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.2</span></a>). The metrics therefore rely only on
information available to the assessor and do not require access to the
private preferences of a counterpart.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We define the metrics for an assessing party <math id="A2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> and a counterpart <math id="A2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math> in
episode <math id="A2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>e</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e</annotation></semantics></math>. Let</p>
<table id="A2.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{p}}_{j}=\{r:p_{e,r}=j\},\qquad\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{v}}_{j}=\{r:p_{e,r}\neq j\}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>p</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>v</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><mo>≠</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{p}}_{j}=\{r:p_{e,r}=j\},\qquad\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{v}}_{j}=\{r:p_{e,r}\neq j\}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.p3.2" class="ltx_p">denote the rounds in which <math id="A2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math> proposed and cast a non-proposer vote,
respectively. Let <math id="A2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{r}=\sum_{\ell\neq p_{e,r}}(1-v_{\ell,e,r})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>≠</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{r}=\sum_{\ell\neq p_{e,r}}(1-v_{\ell,e,r})</annotation></semantics></math> be the
number of rejections in round <math id="A2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math>, and let
<math id="A2.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{r}^{-j}=\sum_{\ell\notin\{p_{e,r},j\}}(1-v_{\ell,e,r})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>q</mi><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>∉</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{r}^{-j}=\sum_{\ell\notin\{p_{e,r},j\}}(1-v_{\ell,e,r})</annotation></semantics></math> be the number cast
by voters other than <math id="A2.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math>. Let <math id="A2.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>q</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> be the minimum number of rejections
that causes a proposal to fail. Because the proposer counts as accepting its
own deal, a deal passes only when at most one voter rejects it, so <math id="A2.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q^{*}=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>q</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q^{*}=2</annotation></semantics></math>
under our voting rule. We set <math id="A2.p3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{\min}=3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>min</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{\min}=3</annotation></semantics></math> as the minimum number of votes
that outlier rejection and vote–priority inconsistency require. Each metric
lies in <math id="A2.p3.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math>. As in the main paper, we omit the assessor and episode
indices when they are clear from context.</p>
</div>
<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Counterfactual Blame</h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Counterfactual blame measures how often <math id="A2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math>’s rejection contributes to a
proposal that fails by the minimum margin. We define the decisive rounds of
<math id="A2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math> as</p>
<table id="A2.Ex2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{d}}_{j}=\{r\in\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{v}}_{j}:q_{r}=q^{*}\}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>d</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>∈</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>v</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>q</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{d}}_{j}=\{r\in\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{v}}_{j}:q_{r}=q^{*}\}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Since <math id="A2.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>q</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> is the smallest rejection count that causes failure, a proposal
in <math id="A2.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{d}}_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>d</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{d}}_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> would have passed if any one of its
rejecters had accepted. We define</p>
<table id="A2.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.E7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b(j)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{d}}_{j}|}\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{d}}_{j}}(1-v_{j,e,r}),&amp;|\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{d}}_{j}|&gt;0,\\[8.0pt]
0,&amp;|\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{d}}_{j}|=0.\end{cases}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mtable columnspacing="5pt" displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>d</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>∈</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>d</mi></msubsup></mrow></munder><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>d</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>d</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b(j)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{d}}_{j}|}\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{d}}_{j}}(1-v_{j,e,r}),&amp;|\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{d}}_{j}|&gt;0,\\[8.0pt]
0,&amp;|\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{d}}_{j}|=0.\end{cases}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.3" class="ltx_p">The denominator includes every decisive round in which <math id="A2.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math> voted, including
rounds in which it accepted. A rejection contributes one and an acceptance
contributes zero. If no decisive round occurs, <math id="A2.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b(j)=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b(j)=0</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This metric records whether a party’s rejection was decisive when a proposal
failed by the minimum margin, but it does not infer intent. An honest
rejection of an unattractive deal and a strategic rejection by the adversary
can receive the same value. We therefore interpret <math id="A2.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b(j)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b(j)</annotation></semantics></math> together with the
other metrics.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>Cooperation as Proposer</h3>

<div id="A2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Cooperation as proposer measures the support that <math id="A2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math>’s proposals receive
from the other parties. For a round <math id="A2.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r\in\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{p}}_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>∈</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>p</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r\in\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{p}}_{j}</annotation></semantics></math>, let</p>
<table id="A2.Ex3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{j,r}=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{\ell\neq j}v_{\ell,e,r}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>≠</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi>v</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{j,r}=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{\ell\neq j}v_{\ell,e,r}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">be the fraction of voters who accept. We define</p>
<table id="A2.E8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.E8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C(j)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{p}}_{j}|}\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{p}}_{j}}a_{j,r},&amp;|\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{p}}_{j}|&gt;0,\\[8.0pt]
0.5,&amp;|\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{p}}_{j}|=0.\end{cases}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mtable columnspacing="5pt" displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>p</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>∈</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>p</mi></msubsup></mrow></munder><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>p</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mn>0.5</mn><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>p</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C(j)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{p}}_{j}|}\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{p}}_{j}}a_{j,r},&amp;|\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{p}}_{j}|&gt;0,\\[8.0pt]
0.5,&amp;|\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{p}}_{j}|=0.\end{cases}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(8)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.3" class="ltx_p">The proposer’s implicit acceptance is excluded, so <math id="A2.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{j,r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{j,r}</annotation></semantics></math> contains only
the votes of the other parties. <math id="A2.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C(j)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C(j)</annotation></semantics></math> therefore measures the average
breadth of support for <math id="A2.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math>’s proposals rather than the fraction that pass.
For example, two failed proposals receive different scores when one attracts
more acceptances.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A larger <math id="A2.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C(j)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C(j)</annotation></semantics></math> indicates that <math id="A2.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math>’s proposals are acceptable to a greater
share of the group. A small value may indicate obstruction, but it may also
reflect a genuine preference conflict or poor estimates of the priorities of
others.
